subject: Business Models
title: Cost-Plus Pricing
description: A fast breakdown of Cost-Plus Pricing for builders.

hook.text: Calculate your costs, add a markup, and that's the price. Simple, predictable, boring.

buildup.text: Government contractors love cost-plus. They bill actual costs plus an agreed profit percentage.

discovery.text: The fatal flaw: cost-plus rewards inefficiency. Higher costs mean higher absolute profit.

twist.text: $640 toilet seats for the Pentagon. Cost-plus pricing with no incentive to cut spending.

climax.text: Most competitive businesses abandoned cost-plus for value-based pricing decades ago.

punchline.text: Higher costs, higher profit. Cost-plus has perverse incentives.

quiz.question: What is the key problem with cost-plus pricing?

details.summary: Cost-plus pricing calculates the total cost of producing a product or service and adds a fixed percentage markup to determine the selling price. A manufacturer with $50 in costs and a 40% markup sells at $70. It is the simplest and most common pricing approach in traditional industries.
details.whyItMatters: Cost-plus pricing guarantees a minimum margin on every sale but ignores customer willingness to pay and competitor dynamics..
takeaways: Price equals total production cost plus a fixed percentage markup
Simple to calculate but ignores what customers are willing to pay
Common in manufacturing, construction, and government contracting

faq.question: When is cost-plus pricing the appropriate strategy?
faq.answer: Cost-plus works best for commoditized products where differentiation is minimal, government contracts that require cost transparency, custom manufacturing with variable inputs, and businesses where cost certainty matters more than margin maximization.

faq.question: What are the key problems with cost-plus pricing?
faq.answer: It ignores customer willingness to pay, potentially leaving enormous value on the table. It does not account for competitive pricing. It penalizes efficiency because lower costs mean lower absolute margins. It fails for digital products where marginal costs are near zero.
